title: Strands Decider 2B: Benchmarks and Limits (2026)
summary: Strands decider returns structured data for AI automation tasks instead of text. Find what changed, when it launched, and how it affects your workflows.
body_markdown:
## Connect Strands Decider to your workflow


You can reach Strands Decider through three general building blocks, simplest first, but nothing native exists and none of them has been tested with it.


On 2026-11-11 the catalog showed no integration built for it, so each route works only if the maker's interface allows it, and running your own tasks through whichever you pick is how you find out.


### Connect Strands Decider with an HTTP request step


If the maker publishes an endpoint that accepts a task and returns a decision, a plain HTTP request step is enough.


The first assumption to break is the response shape: if the decision comes back as free text rather than a fixed field, every downstream step ends up parsing prose.


Fix it at the boundary by requiring structured output, or by adding one validation step that rejects anything off-schema, rather than patching each consumer.


### Use Strands Decider as an OpenAI-compatible AI step


This route needs the maker to expose an OpenAI-compatible chat interface, or your tool to accept a custom provider with a base URL and key. Check tool calling and structured output first, since compatible in name often covers only basic completions.


If either is missing, you get a model that answers but can't drive your steps.


Switching to Route 1 is cleaner than stacking prompt workarounds on a partial interface.


### Connect Strands Decider through an MCP server


This needs the maker to ship an MCP server, or to offer an interface you can wrap in one. It's the most work because you own the tool definitions, the authentication, and the failure handling.


Keep the exposed tools narrow: one wrapper per decision type, with typed inputs. A single catch-all tool only moves the mess into the prompt.


Whichever route you choose, the connection tells you nothing about quality; that comes from the measurement that follows. It does settle one wiring question, though: whether the Decider connection has to be built twice, once for flows and once for agents.


In Activepieces it doesn't, because a integration is an agent tool the moment it's connected.


The same integration action that runs as a step in a flow is exposed as a tool schema on the project's MCP server, where Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or an agent you built yourself can call it.


So an HTTP step or provider wrapper for Decider needs no separate catalog to publish to and no export step; a catalog you have to re-integrate for your agents is a second migration.


The Integrations Framework and MCP Server documentation describe the mechanism, and packages/integrations in the open source repo shows it.
